subject: Advanced constraints in mirt (user-defined parameters etc.)

messages.author: 498625331dc5ad8c
messages.subject: Advanced constraints in mirt (user-defined parameters etc.)
parts:
Hello,
I wonder if there is any possibility in mirt to set up user-defined parameters or advanced constraints, which are well known in traditional IRT/SEM software like Mplus (or lavaan). Is there any possibility to include a completely new parameter in the parameter table, or to set up more complicated constraints like parameters a+b+c+d = 0? I needed this in the last days so much that I was thinking of switching to SEM parameterization in Mplus or lavaan, but I don't want it :) I also tried to introduce the so-called "phantom variables", but this did not work very well.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Advanced constraints in mirt (user-defined parameters etc.)
parts:
There is some support for this, which I've demonstrated in this vignette. Basically, it requires you to locate the parameters that are of interest, establish the constraints you're interested in via R functions, and use one of R's more sophisticated estimation algorithms (e.g., from the nloptr package). More involved parameters constraints like these are less common in IRT modeling, which is why the package doesn't currently have an abstracted syntax approach (if there's more interest in the future that could change, however). HTH.

Phil

messages.author: 498625331dc5ad8c
messages.subject: Re: Advanced constraints in mirt (user-defined parameters etc.)
parts:
Oh, that's amazing! I am going to try it immediately! Thank you very much. I know these constraints are less common under IRT, but I think this is a pity. For example, I needed to set up measurement invariance across the response scale with different labels ("agree/slightly agree/..." vs. "strongly agree/agree/..."), which cannot be done without it. The same I needed for differentiation of metric and scalar invariance in GPCM model as I need to distinguish item thresholds and total item difficulty. (This is possible with a graded rating scale model, GRSM, which is equivalent to the traditional graded model, but not with GPCM, which I wanted to use in the case.) 

Anyway, can I have one more unrelated question? I am estimating M2* statistics in the multigroup confirmatory IRT model, and some items are completely omitted in some groups. In such a case, M2/M2*/C2 obviously fails. I, therefore, computed SRMSR manually, eliminating particular variables. I also used a so-called phantom variable and randomly imputed data (and some constraints plus d.f. adjustment) to got a cross-product matrix. However, as I cannot use residual centering with nominal data, it is still slightly biased and I am afraid how I will able to explain the complicated and (probably unnecessary) approach to reviewers :) Is there any need to use all of the variables in each group? I tried to upgrade M2 function and exclude particular variables (and its parameters) from the computation based on user choice, but I have got lost, and I am not sure if it could even work :) Do you think so? Or is there something I am missing?

messages.subject: Re: Advanced constraints in mirt (user-defined parameters etc.)
parts:
It works great! :) Unfortunately, I tried both solnp and  nloptr, but it seems that I cannot release latent variance on some groups if I don't use Rasch model:
model1_metric <- "
SE=1-10
FREE [5] = (1, d0)
"
eqfun_metric <- function(p, optim_args) {
  res1_1 <- p[42:44]-p[2:4]-p[41]
  res1_1
}
solnp_args <- list(eqfun=eqfun_metric, eqB=rep(0, 3))
test.metric <- multipleGroup(dat5[2:11], model1, SE=F, itemtype = "gpcm", technical = technical, 
                             group = as.factor(dat5$dataset),
                             invariance = c("slopes", "free_var"), 
                             optimizer = 'solnp', solnp_args=solnp_args, pars=sv) 

Error: Error in diag(sqrt(diag(gp$gcov))) : 
  invalid 'nrow' value (too large or NA)
In addition: Warning message:
In sqrt(diag(gp$gcov)) : NaNs produced
functionsdsd
sdsd
(Latent variance is identified, of course). But thank you, this was really useful!
